country.comment: Empirical narratives and meeting/interview extracts focus on the Breede-Overberg Water Management Area in the Western Cape, South Africa (including the Ruensveld and Duivenhoks commercial farming areas, the fishing village of Kassiesbaai in Arniston/Waenhuiskrans, and Matroosberg farm schools).
country.where_found: PDF p. 1, Title, Abstract, Section 1.1; PDF p. 4, Section 4

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative synthesis of comparative case narratives, interview quotes, and participatory meeting discourse; national baseline figures (~8 million lacking adequate water and ~38% without adequate sanitation in 2003, PDF p. 2) and historical infrastructure figures (1,400 km farmer pipeline network, PDF p. 5) are descriptive context rather than statistical effect estimates.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Despite post-apartheid statutory reforms mandating decentralized multi-stakeholder participation under the Water Services Act (Act 108 of 1997) and National Water Act (Act 36 of 1998) via Catchment Management Agencies (CMAs) and Water User Associations (WUAs), implementation in the Breede-Overberg Water Management Area remains top-down and dominated by technical discourse and pre-existing white commercial farming networks (which historically secured a 1,400 km rural pipeline network across 540,000 hectares). Unequal technical knowledge, preset agendas, bureaucratic dismissal of non-technical input, distrust, and feelings of shame silence marginalized black and colored residents and local councilors (such as in Kassiesbaai, ~230 households), keeping basic domestic water supply, water quality, and sanitation needs off formal water management agendas and reproducing exclusion.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 2–3, Section 1.2; PDF pp. 4–8, Section 4; PDF pp. 9–15, Sections 6–7; PDF p. 16, Section 8

mechanism_certainty.comment: Capped at 2 by the qualitative study design ceiling (CASP Qualitative Checklist). Rated 2 because the study directly observes and documents the administrative/participatory mechanism through verbatim extracts from Breede-Overberg CMA/WMA public participation meetings and interviews with local councilors, a small-scale farmer, officials, and consultants, showing how technical framing, information overload, preset agendas, and bureaucratic 'fobbing off' silence marginalized representatives and exclude basic domestic water and sanitation issues from formal decision-making.
mechanism_certainty.where_found: PDF pp. 6–7, Section 4.2; PDF pp. 9–15, Sections 6–7

mechanism_flags.comment: Central mechanism is multi-stakeholder participation in CMAs/WUAs and local consultations (participation), alongside state-society lobbying and councilor-municipality representation networks (political_coordination), proliferation of apartheid water authorities and the institutional split between CMA technical resource management and basic domestic service delivery (institutional_fragmentation), bureaucratic agenda control, technical framing, and dismissal of lay concerns in participatory forums (discretion), catchment/WMA water planning (planning), and the 1996 abolition of riparian water rights tied to private land ownership as well as landless farmworkers' exclusion (property).

sample_size.comment: The paper contains no standalone methods section and does not report the total number of interviews conducted or participatory meetings observed. Empirically, it examines 1 Water Management Area (Breede-Overberg WMA) through 2 contrasting local case narratives (commercial farming in Ruensveld/Duivenhoks and the fishing village of Kassiesbaai, which comprises approximately 230 households [250 households noted on the Fishermen's Union plot in Footnote 9]) and quotes individual qualitative interviews and DWAF/WMA meetings from 2001–2004.
